clue.text: Was rich, as heartless 6 concluded?

indicators.note: heartless asks for the two central letters of the phrase to be cut out

parts.note: the answer to 6 down, meaning a fight
concluded means ended

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person grew wealthy when an unfeeling bout reached its end.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 is the answer ABOUT; 'heartless' removes the middle TE from ABOUT ENDED.
explanation.definitionFit: To abound is to be plentiful, so something that abounded was rich in supply.

clue.text: Get female in? Nearly

indicators.note: nearly means the last letter of the phrase is dropped

parts.note: someone in is at home

explanation.surface: A doorkeeper wonders whether to let a woman inside, and almost does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' trims the final E from AT HOME.
explanation.definitionFit: To fathom something is to understand it, as in 'I don't get it'.

clue.text: Palette's content? I slap it on all over the place

indicators.note: all over the place says these letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A slapdash painter describes how colours go onto the canvas from the palette.
explanation.definitionFit: Artists mix coloured pigment in linseed on a palette before brushing it on.

clue.text: Overcomes the same again in ways where resistance is futile

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other
if resistance is futile it counts for nothing, so its letter is taken away

parts.note: routes are ways
R is the symbol for electrical resistance
DO, short for ditto, means the same again

explanation.surface: A Borg-like warning that whoever keeps repeating themselves wins where resistance is pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resistance is futile' is the Borg catchphrase from Star Trek, here signalling that R goes; 'in' then places the ditto mark inside what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: To outdo a rival is to surpass or beat them.

clue.text: On-side shot's a feature of today

definitions.meaning: in cricket the leg side is the on side, and a pull is a shot played there
the puzzle ran on April Fool's Day, when hoaxes and practical jokes are traditional

explanation.definitionFit: A pull to leg is a cricket stroke, and a leg-pull is a teasing hoax typical of April Fool's Day.

clue.text: Engaged in a fight

parts.note: a bout is a boxing fight

explanation.surface: Someone is busy taking part in a punch-up.
explanation.definitionFit: To be about something is to be busy with it, as in 'while you're at it'.

clue.text: Many expressions of doubt, in an everyday sense?

indicators.note: in places the two sounds inside the word for sense

parts.note: nous is British slang for common, practical sense
um is a hesitant sound of doubt
er is another hesitant sound of doubt

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether repeated doubts belong to everyday common sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Numerous means great in number, plenty.

clue.text: Nothing sinister about this crime writer?

definitions.meaning: in heraldry sinister is left and its opposite, the right side
Colin ... wrote the Inspector Morse detective novels

explanation.definitionFit: Dexter is the heraldic right, the opposite of sinister, and Colin Dexter created Inspector Morse.

clue.text: Now leave, due new happiness

parts.note: beat it is a slang order to go away now

indicators.note: new signals the following word being made over in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Someone is told to clear off, owing a fresh sort of joy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' turns DUE into UDE, added to BEAT IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Beatitude is supreme blessedness or bliss.

clue.text: Check back and front of Englishman — Sheila's bloke?

indicators.note: back says the word for check is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: to curb is to check or restrain

indicators.note: front of picks just the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: An Australian woman inspects an Englishman from behind and in front: is he her man?
explanation.walkthrough: In Australian slang a sheila is a woman and Bruce the stereotypical Aussie male name.
explanation.definitionFit: Bruce is the jokey stock name for an Australian man, the partner of a stereotypical Sheila.

clue.text: Heads up, sadly typical of United's left side

indicators.note: sadly suggests the letters are in a sorry, jumbled state and need rearranging

explanation.surface: Football fans are told to keep their chins up despite the poor form of United's left flank.
explanation.walkthrough: United's left side is its first letter, U, whose shape the answer describes.
explanation.definitionFit: The letter U at the left of 'United' has the curved form of a horseshoe.

clue.text: Prig has no time to be cautious

parts.note: a prude is a prim, priggish person
N is an abbreviation for no, as on a yes/no form

explanation.surface: A self-righteous person has no time for being careful.
explanation.definitionFit: Prudent means careful and wise in judgement.

clue.text: Using seed, 24 replaces fish fly

indicators.note: replaces read as re-places, putting the letters in new positions

parts.note: the answer to 24 down, a sailors' night out

explanation.surface: An angler using seed bait swaps one fish for an insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 is MOLLIE; 'replaces' (re-places) shuffles it with SEED.
explanation.definitionFit: Demoiselle names both the damselfish and the damselfly, so it is a word for a fish and a fly.

clue.text: Solvers' year belonging to The Independent

parts.note: from the newspaper's own viewpoint, what belongs to it is ours

explanation.surface: A newspaper claims its readers' year belongs to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition addresses the solvers directly: what belongs to you.
explanation.definitionFit: Addressing solvers as 'you', what is the solvers' is yours.

clue.text: Cleverly, one can infiltrate evil enemy from ancient city

indicators.note: cleverly hints the whole lot is artfully rearranged
infiltrate says the first two words slip in among the enemy's letters, joining one mixed pool
evil suggests the letters of enemy are corrupted into a new order

parts.note: A is a word for one

explanation.surface: A clever agent slips in among a wicked foe from an old city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleverly', 'infiltrate' and 'evil' together tell you to mix A and CAN into ENEMY and rearrange the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Mycenae was a Bronze Age Greek city, and its adjective describes people or things from there.

clue.text: Expand on letter from Greece covering comeback

indicators.note: comeback says the combined letters are read backwards

parts.note: eta is a letter of the Greek alphabet
a lid is a covering

explanation.surface: Elaborate on a Greek letter that deals with someone's return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comeback' governs both pieces, so the whole string is read backwards; 'on' belongs with 'Expand' in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To dilate on a subject is to speak or write at length about it.

clue.text: The learned American's quantity drunk for lunch?

parts.note: liter is the American spelling of the unit of volume
at one o'clock, I being the Roman numeral for one, is lunchtime

explanation.surface: An American asks how much he drinks with his midday meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is a liter drunk at I (one o'clock), the usual lunch hour.
explanation.definitionFit: The literati are well-read, educated people, the intelligentsia.

clue.text: Pain in toto creates necessity for plaster?

parts.note: gyp is British slang for pain, as in 'my knee is giving me gyp'
in toto means in total, the sum

explanation.surface: Total agony makes one need a plaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaster of Paris is made by heating this mineral, so it is essential to the material.

clue.text: Writer's heading for north archipelago to promote first of novels, nothing major of note

indicators.note: in a down clue heading north means read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: the writer's is I'm, short for I am

indicators.note: promote means a letter is moved up to the top of the word

parts.note: Orkney is an archipelago off the north of Scotland

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A novelist heads to Scotland's northern islands to publicise a debut book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading for north' turns I'M into MI; 'to promote' moves N to the front of ORKNEY, giving NORKEY.
explanation.definitionFit: A minor key is a musical mode set against the major, so a key that is no major one.

clue.text: Revolting demirep paid by the day

indicators.note: revolting means turning over, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A disgusting woman of doubtful repute is paid daily.
explanation.walkthrough: A demirep is a woman of doubtful reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Per diem is Latin for 'for each day', used of allowances given daily.

clue.text: Translator has disagreement about what may contribute to fugue

indicators.note: about means the quarrel goes round the translator

parts.note: a set-to is a quarrel

explanation.surface: A translator quarrels over the parts of a fugue.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretto is the overlapping of entries of the subject, a classic device in a fugue's closing section.

clue.text: France worried about cheese?

parts.note: F is the international vehicle code for France

indicators.note: about says the word for worried is turned round

parts.note: ate, as in 'what's eating you', means worried

explanation.surface: France fretting over its cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Feta is a white brined Greek cheese.

clue.text: Starve poisson d'avril, perhaps, in the morning breaks

indicators.note: breaks means the morning abbreviation cuts into the fish

parts.note: poisson d'avril, French April fool, is literally an April fish
AM means in the morning

explanation.surface: Starve the April fool at daybreak.
explanation.definitionFit: To famish is to make extremely hungry, to starve.

clue.text: Australian Army overcoming the heat in congested city — I may have predicted this

indicators.note: in places the whole inside the city

parts.note: the Great Wen was William Cobbett's name for overcrowded London

indicators.note: overcoming means the two letters surround the unit of heat

parts.note: a therm is a unit of heat

explanation.surface: Aussie troops beat the heat in a crowded city, which someone claims to have forecast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overcoming' puts the two A's round the unit of heat; 'in' sets the result inside London's old nickname. The definition leans on the clue: a forecaster may well have predicted the heat.
explanation.definitionFit: A weather forecaster predicts heat, rain and the like.

clue.text: Following Mayor's lead, Hardy's making merry

indicators.note: lead picks the opening letter of the word

parts.note: Ollie was the nickname of Oliver Hardy of Laurel and Hardy

explanation.surface: Following the mayor, a Wessex novelist turns jovial.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy is not Thomas Hardy but Oliver, called Ollie.
explanation.definitionFit: In old sailors' slang a mollie was a night of carousing, a spree.

clue.text: Piped water a factor in oedema, in short

indicators.note: factor in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Tap water may contribute to swelling, put briefly.
explanation.definitionFit: The mains supply delivers piped water to buildings.

clue.text: Theatre operating a dimmer switch?

indicators.note: switch means the letters change places

explanation.surface: Stage crew working the lighting switch.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mermaid is a London theatre; 'operating' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mermaid Theatre is a playhouse at Blackfriars in London.

clue.text: Always, as the poet has it, end in Amazon?

indicators.note: in puts the word for end inside

parts.words: Always, as the poet has it
parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, always
a tail is an end

explanation.surface: Poetic musing on whether things always end up in the Amazon jungle.
explanation.definitionFit: Amazon is an example of an online retailer.

clue.text: Demonstrated lustrous silk

definitions.meaning: protesters demonstrate when they occupy a place in a sit-in

explanation.surface: Protesters showed off glossy fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Protesters who held a sit-in demonstrated, and a glossy weave of silk has the same spelling.

clue.text: Hand over a 8 criminal, securing just the ticket

indicators.note: securing means holding the other piece inside
criminal indicates the letters are rearranged lawlessly

parts.note: a, plus the answer to 8 down, the crime writer
it means exactly the right thing, as in 'that's it'

explanation.surface: A crime writer's villain must be handed over, ticket in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' reworks A plus the 8 down answer into EXTRADE; 'securing' wraps those letters round 'it'.
explanation.definitionFit: To extradite is to surrender a suspect to another state's jurisdiction.
